request.system:
You are assisting with the qualitative analysis of interview data from a study of frontline hotel employees' work experiences. You will receive one passage from an interview transcript. Code the passage as a qualitative researcher would in first-order coding, and complete the coding form below.

About the passage
- The passage begins with brief details about the interviewee: role, gender and years in the job.
- Lines marked "Interviewer:" are the interviewer's questions. Lines marked "Interviewee:" are the interviewee's answers.
- Some passages contain two excerpts from the same interview, marked [Earlier in the interview] and [Later in the interview].

The coding form
1. codes: Give between 3 and 6 first-order codes. Each code has a short label of 2 to 6 words, kept close to the interviewee's own language, and one supporting quote. Each quote must be copied word for word from the passage, without any change, and must be no longer than 30 words.
2. interpretation: In one or two sentences, in your own words, state what the interviewee is communicating in this passage.
3. tone: The overall tone of the interviewee's account. Choose one: positive, negative, mixed or neutral.
4. confidence: An integer from 0 to 100 indicating how confident you are that your interpretation is accurate.

Respond only with a JSON object that follows the schema provided. Write in English.
request.user:
Interviewee details: Room attendant, male, 11th year

Interviewer: Your floor got a new team leader this year. How is everyone getting on with her?

Interviewee: The new team leader is a young woman born after 1995, poached from another hotel. I heard she was known over there for being strict. She’s not much older than my daughter. She’s extremely particular: pillow corners have to line up, the folded edge of the bath towel has to face outwards, and when she inspects a room she shines a torch under the bed. In eleven years nobody had ever checked my work like that. The old team leader would take one look and sign off. For the first month I went home every day and complained to my wife: this girl is far too fussy, she has no human touch at all, she’ll drive everyone out sooner or later. Later I found that she inspects carefully but doesn’t know how to be flexible. Two rooms on our floor had a smell coming out of the air-conditioning vents for ages. I told her several times that we should report it to Engineering. She said we should just clean the rooms to standard first, and the rest wasn’t our business. In the end a guest complained, and the penalty points went against us. She didn’t say a single word on our behalf. When I went to ask her about it, she told me to look up a page number in the standards manual. The week she handled her first group inspection, I applied to move to the fourteenth floor and swapped shifts with another long-serving colleague. Now I’m not under her. When we see each other we say hello and that’s it, and we don’t sit at the same table at mealtimes either. Everyone knows how things stand, and the manager knows the two of us don’t get on, so he keeps us on different shifts as much as he can. Next month she’s being transferred to the new branch as a supervisor. The manager asked us if we had any comments about her. I said not really. To be honest, she is capable, and she inspects rooms more thoroughly than anyone, but she and I just don’t get along. With her gone, things on our floor will be a bit easier. Everyone thinks so.
